procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of detention passed on June 12, 1971, under sub-s. (1) read with sub-s. (3) of s. 3 of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, directing the petitioner's detention.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not mentioned in the provided text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Original Jurisdiction: Writ Petition No. 77 of 1972 under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for a writ in the nature of habeas corpus. The petition failed and was dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the ground of detention concerning causing injuries with a sword was an extraneous ground that would invalidate the detention order, on the basis that it only constituted an offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code and did not fall under the definition required by the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
One of the grounds for detention (Ground No. 2) was that the petitioner and his associates assaulted a person with a sword, causing injuries, and then terrorized the public by brandishing the weapon.

The petitioner argued that this ground was extraneous because causing injury with a sword is an offense under Section 324 of the Penal Code, which does not carry a severe enough penalty to qualify under the West Bengal Act.
law: Under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, Section 3(2)(d) defines acts that are considered prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.
The Arms Act, 1959, Section 2(1)(c), defines 'arms' to include sharp-edged and other deadly weapons.
Possessing arms, such as a sword, without a license where one is required by a government notification, is an offense punishable with imprisonment under the Arms Act, 1959.

Section 24 of the General Clauses Act provides that notifications issued under a repealed act (like the Arms Act of 1878) can continue to be in force under a new, re-enacted act (like the Arms Act of 1959).
application: The Court rejected the petitioner's argument by analyzing the act not just as an assault under the Penal Code, but as an offense under the Arms Act, 1959.
First, the Court established that a sword is legally defined as 'arms' under Section 2(1)(c) of the Arms Act.
Next, it found that a government notification requiring a license for such weapons, issued under the previous Arms Act of 1878, was still in force by virtue of Section 24 of the General Clauses Act.
Therefore, possessing and carrying a sword without a license was an offense under the Arms Act, 1959.

The Court reasoned that since the petitioner's actions constituted an offense under the Arms Act, 1959, they were covered by the definition of prejudicial acts in Section 3(2)(d) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the ground of detention concerning the sword attack was not extraneous. It was a valid ground because the act constituted an offense under the Arms Act, 1959, which fell within the scope of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970. Consequently, the detention order was not invalidated.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the ground of detention concerning causing injuries with a sword was an extraneous ground that would invalidate the detention order, on the basis that it only constituted an offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code and did not fall under the definition required by the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
appellant_arguments: The activity set out in ground of detention No. 2, namely causing injuries with a sword, constitutes an offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code.
An offence under Section 324 is not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment for a term of seven years.
Therefore, this ground does not fall under the definition of activities prejudicial to public order as defined in the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
As this ground is extraneous to the Act, it renders the entire detention order invalid.
respondent_arguments: The act of causing injuries with a sword also constitutes an offence under the Arms Act, 1959, for being in possession of and carrying a sword without a license.
An offence under the Arms Act, 1959, falls under clause (d) of Section 3(2) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
Therefore, the ground of detention is not extraneous to the Act and the detention order is valid.

cases.case_name: Chief Inspector of Mines v. Lala Karam Chand Thapar
cases.principle: For the construction of s. 24 of the General Clauses Act, meaning that when an earlier Act is repealed by a later Act which re-enacts the provisions of the earlier Act, Regulations framed under the repealed Act continue in force and are deemed to have been made under the provisions so re-enacted, and must be construed as having continuity of force.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Pursuant to Section 24 of the General Clauses Act, when an earlier Act is repealed and its provisions are re-enacted by a later Act, any notification or regulation made under the repealed Act continues in force and is deemed to have been made under the re-enacted provisions of the new Act, unless the new Act expresses a contrary intention or the notification is superseded by one issued under the new Act.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the ground of detention concerning causing injuries with a sword was not extraneous to the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970. While the act may constitute an offence under the Penal Code, it also constitutes an offence under the Arms Act, 1959, for possessing and carrying a sword without a license. Since offences under the Arms Act are explicitly included as a basis for detention under Section 3(2)(d) of the West Bengal Act, the ground was valid and did not invalidate the detention order.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation of Section 3(2)(d) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, which defines acts prejudicial to public order to include offences under the Arms Act, 1959.
Statutory interpretation of Section 2(1)(c) of the Arms Act, 1959, to determine if a sword qualifies as an 'arm'.
Application of Section 24 of the General Clauses Act to determine if a notification issued under a repealed Act continues in force under the re-enacted statute.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that the act only constituted an offence under Section 324 of the Penal Code was too narrow and failed to consider that the same act also constituted an offence under the Arms Act, 1959.

The court determined that an offence under the Arms Act, 1959, is explicitly listed as a valid ground for detention under clause (d) of Section 3(2) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970.
Therefore, the appellant's argument that the ground was extraneous to the Act failed, as the act fell squarely within the statutory definition of activities prejudicial to public order.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully argued that the act of causing injuries with a sword also constituted an offence under the Arms Act, 1959.
The court agreed with this reasoning, finding that a sword is an 'arm' under the definition in Section 2(1)(c) of the Arms Act, and its possession and carrying without a license is an offence.

Because an offence under the Arms Act is a specified ground for detention in Section 3(2)(d) of the West Bengal Act, the court concluded that the ground was not extraneous and the detention order was valid.
